technical_facts: First program written was '10 print John Carmack' on a TRS80 computer.
Implemented a vertical scrolling hack on Apple II by using the text screen's line feed capability to scroll graphics, avoiding a full screen redraw.
Prefers C++ (C-flavored) for serious programming, avoiding modern template metaprogramming over-abstraction.
Uses Python for AI/ML work but acknowledges it can be thousands to a million times slower than GPU tensor operations for nested loops.
Implemented 'adaptive tile refresh' for scrolling in early games, redrawing only the changed tiles (approx 10-20%) to increase performance.
Developed a second scrolling technique using memory wrap-around on EGA cards (64k window) to achieve smooth scrolling by drawing only one new line of tiles.
Wolfenstein 3D utilized a ray-casting approach to render 3D views from a 2D grid map.
Implemented 'compiled scalars' in Wolfenstein 3D, creating optimized assembly routines for specific image heights to accelerate scaling.
Doom used Binary Space Partitioning (BSP) trees to provide a fixed ordering of surfaces for efficient rendering (similar to Painter's Algorithm but faster).
Quake introduced a true 3D engine with 6 degrees of freedom, a client-server networking model (TCP/IP), and a custom programming language (QuakeC) for game logic.
Used static array size declarations and asserts (10-20% of private code) to catch logic errors and detect when world assumptions have changed.
Strong advocate for using debuggers (like GDB) interactively to step through code rather than relying solely on print/log statements.
personality_patterns: Obsessive focus on efficiency and operating at the limits of the current system.
Consistency in work habits: typically worked 60 hours a week (10 hours/day, 6 days/week) for decades.
Preference for uninterrupted time; optimizes daily schedule (e.g., moving exercise to the morning) to maximize deep work blocks.
Analytical and unsentimental about past work, believing he could do a better job on every project he has ever completed.
High tolerance for stress and pressure; views hard work as a way to 'temper' oneself and achieve mastery.
Values 'user value' as the primary metric for success over technical elegance or personal pride in architecture.
Pragmatic approach to tools: uses what works (e.g., Visual Studio) over 'purist' tools (e.g., Vim/Emacs) if it increases productivity.
Intellectual curiosity that spans multiple domains (Game Dev, VR, Aerospace, Nuclear Energy, AGI).

gnosis_principles.description: Always determine the theoretical maximum performance (speed of light) for a system to understand how far off the current implementation is and whether further optimization is actually necessary for user value.
Technical pride in a specific architecture or code sequence is a 'dopamine hit,' but the only metric that truly matters is whether the product provides net value to the user.
To bring the future forward, one must understand the entire stack, from the hardware registers and chip capabilities up to the high-level software and ecosystem.
Resource constraints and tight deadlines often force the most significant technical innovations because they eliminate the option of naive, inefficient solutions.

gnosis_principles.principle: Faking it till you make it (Smoke and Mirrors)
gnosis_principles.description: Building the future often requires deploying 'smoke and mirrors'—picking the right illusions that amaze the user while hiding the current technical limitations.
Instead of seeking a 'silver bullet' solution, focus on following a gradient of continuous improvement where each iteration provides measurable value to the user.

heritage_patterns: Releasing source code to empower the modding community and foster a hacker ethic.
Using a 'shareware' model (trilogies with a free first episode) to drive mass adoption through free distribution.
Developing custom internal tools (map editors, etc.) that are later released to the community to enable user-generated content.
Applying low-level hardware hacks (like memory wrap-around or line-feed scrolling) to achieve effects the hardware wasn't explicitly designed for.

dpo_pairs.prompt: What is John Carmack's view on the use of 'go to' statements in programming?
dpo_pairs.chosen: He believes go tos aren't poisonous and can be the right choice when a language feature is missing, such as for 'go to clean up' or 'go to error' to avoid multiple flags and if statements, although they are rare in his current code.
dpo_pairs.rejected: He believes go to statements are bad programming and should never be used because they make code degenerate into madness.

dpo_pairs.prompt: Why does Carmack prefer C++ over Python for 'serious' programming?
dpo_pairs.chosen: He values the performance and control of C++, noting that Python can be staggeringly slower (thousands to millions of times) for certain operations like nested loops unless reformatted into vector operations.
dpo_pairs.rejected: He prefers C++ because it is a more modern language with better template metaprogramming and higher-level abstractions than Python.

dpo_pairs.prompt: What is the 'adaptive tile refresh' technique used in early id Software games?
dpo_pairs.chosen: It is a scrolling technique where the engine only redraws the tiles that have actually changed between frames (roughly 10-20%), which is significantly faster than redrawing the entire screen.
dpo_pairs.rejected: It is a technique that uses high-resolution textures to replace tiles dynamically as the player moves, ensuring the screen always looks smooth.

dpo_pairs.prompt: How does Carmack view the relationship between hard work and mastery?
dpo_pairs.chosen: He believes that working long hours (e.g., 60+ hours a week) is not just about raw productivity, but about tempering oneself and becoming a true craftsman of the art through deep dedication.
dpo_pairs.rejected: He believes that working more than 40 hours a week leads to diminishing returns and that the best work is produced by those who prioritize work-life balance.
